core_principles: Squatting and jump-landing movements should primarily utilize sagittal-plane motion across all lower extremity joints to properly absorb and dissipate landing forces.
Adequate ankle dorsiflexion range of motion (DF-ROM) is required to allow forward rotation of the shank at the ankle when the foot is in contact with the ground.

Limitations in ankle dorsiflexion can restrict sagittal-plane motion at the knee and trunk, leading to compensatory frontal- and transverse-plane motions (such as medial knee displacement) that increase ACL injury risk.
Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) loading is maximized when the knee is in a minimally flexed or hyperextended position combined with a large quadriceps contraction.
common_mistakes: Landing in a relatively extended knee position (sagittal plane) combined with frontal- and transverse-plane loading.
Medial knee displacement (dynamic valgus collapse) during overhead squats (OHS), single-leg squats (SLS), or jump landings (JL).
Restricting forward rotation of the shank due to limited ankle dorsiflexion.
specific_findings: Participants displaying medial-knee displacement during an overhead squat (OHS) had approximately 20% less nonweight-bearing (NWB), passive ankle dorsiflexion (DF) than those without displacement.
Medial-knee displacement observed during the OHS was corrected when a 2-in (5.08-cm) lift was placed under the heel.
The study utilized passive-ankle DF-ROM cutoff points of >= 15 degrees for the normal group and <= 5 degrees for the limited group.
Cited data from Moseley et al. classified ankle flexibility as normal (11.2 to 25.0 degrees) or inflexible (4.3 to 11.2 degrees).

exercise_type: Overhead Squat, Single-Leg Squat, and Jump Landing
core_principles: Perform the Overhead Squat (OHS) with feet shoulder-width apart, arms raised vertically overhead, and heels flat on the ground.
Perform the Single-Leg Squat (SLS) with hands on the hips and the non-stance leg raised in front with the foot approximately 10 cm off the ground.
For both OHS and SLS, squat to a depth of at least 60 degrees of knee flexion.
Maintain a controlled cadence during squats using a metronome set to 60 beats per minute (2 beats to descend, 2 beats to return to the starting position).

For the Jump Landing (JL) task, jump horizontally from a 30-cm box placed at a distance of 50% of the participant's standing height, land, and immediately perform a maximum-effort vertical jump without hesitation.
Ensure equal push-off from both feet when leaving the box during the jump landing task.
common_mistakes: Failing to reach at least 60 degrees of knee flexion during the OHS or SLS.
Lifting the heels off the ground during the squatting motion.
Failing to maintain hands overhead during the OHS or hands on hips during the SLS.
Losing balance or failing to maintain the prescribed metronome cadence during the SLS.
Hesitating before the vertical jump phase of the Jump Landing task.
Unequal push-off from the feet when departing the box in the Jump Landing task.
specific_findings: Non-weight-bearing dorsiflexion range of motion (NWB DF-ROM) test demonstrated an intraclass correlation coefficient [3,k] of 0.988 and a standard error of measurement of 0.888.
Weight-bearing lunge (WBL) test demonstrated an intraclass correlation coefficient [3,k] of 0.953 and a standard error of measurement of 1.618.
The mean knee-flexion angle in the starting position was 8 degrees for the OHS and 12 degrees for the SLS.
The Jump Landing task utilized a 30-cm box placed at a distance of exactly 50% of the participant's standing height.
The squatting cadence was standardized using a metronome set at 60 beats/min, requiring 2 beats for descent and 2 beats for ascent.

core_principles: Limited ankle dorsiflexion range of motion (DF-ROM) during weight-bearing lunge (WBL) assessments is associated with altered knee and ankle kinematics during squatting tasks.
Individuals with limited ankle DF-ROM exhibit reduced knee-flexion displacement and reduced ankle-dorsiflexion displacement during both overhead squats (OHS) and single-leg squats (SLS).
Weight-bearing lunge (WBL) measures are more indicative of dynamic movement limitations than non-weight-bearing (NWB) ankle DF-ROM measures.
Adequate ankle mobility is essential for achieving optimal squat depth (peak knee flexion) and proper lower extremity joint displacement.
common_mistakes: Reduced squat depth (less peak knee flexion) caused by restricted ankle mobility.
Inability to achieve sufficient ankle dorsiflexion displacement during the descent phase of squats.
specific_findings: During the Overhead Squat (OHS), the normal group (WBL >= 44.02 degrees) displayed greater knee-flexion displacement (mean difference, 14.94 degrees; P = .001) and greater ankle DF displacement (mean difference, 7.89 degrees; P < .001) compared with the limited group (WBL <= 44.01 degrees).

During the Single-Leg Squat (SLS), the normal group demonstrated greater knee-flexion displacement (mean difference, 12.39 degrees; P = .001), greater ankle DF displacement (mean difference = 6.44 degrees; P < .001), and greater knee-varus displacement (mean difference, 5.50 degrees; P = .048) than the limited group.
The normal group demonstrated greater peak knee flexion during the OHS (normal, 112.71 +/- 13.48 degrees; limited, 97.45 +/- 14.34 degrees; mean difference, 15.26 degrees; P = .001).
The normal group demonstrated greater peak knee flexion during the SLS (normal, 88.71 +/- 12.73 degrees; limited, 77.09 +/- 10.20 degrees; mean difference, 11.62 degrees; P = .003).
70% (28 of 40) of participants remained in the same group (normal or limited) for both ankle DF-ROM assessments (NWB and WBL).
No significant differences were observed between the NWB DF-ROM groups during the OHS, SLS, or JL tasks for any joint-displacement variable.

core_principles: Limited ankle dorsiflexion range of motion (DF-ROM) during a weight-bearing lunge (WBL) alters knee- and ankle-joint kinematics during squatting.
Individuals with limited ankle DF-ROM display reduced knee-flexion displacement during squatting tasks.
Individuals with limited ankle DF-ROM display reduced ankle-dorsiflexion displacement during squatting tasks.
common_mistakes: Reduced knee flexion during squatting due to limited ankle mobility.
Reduced ankle dorsiflexion displacement during squatting.

core_principles: Ankle dorsiflexion range of motion directly impacts knee flexion displacement during both overhead and single-legged squats.
Individuals with limited ankle dorsiflexion exhibit significantly reduced knee flexion (shallower squat depth) and reduced ankle dorsiflexion displacement during squatting tasks.
The weight-bearing lunge assessment is a strong indicator of kinematic limitations during functional squatting patterns.
common_mistakes: Achieving insufficient squat depth (reduced knee flexion) due to restricted ankle mobility.
Inability to achieve adequate ankle dorsiflexion displacement during overhead or single-legged squats.
specific_findings: In the weight-bearing lunge assessment for overhead squats, the normal group (n = 20) achieved knee flexion of 103.94 +/- 11.79 degrees compared to 89.00 +/- 14.62 degrees in the limited group (n = 20) (P < 0.001, Effect Size = 1.31).

In the weight-bearing lunge assessment for overhead squats, ankle dorsiflexion displacement was -32.03 +/- 6.36 degrees for the normal group versus -24.14 +/- 4.27 degrees for the limited group (P < 0.001, Effect Size = 1.49).

For single-legged squats, the weight-bearing lunge normal group (n = 20) achieved knee flexion of 76.36 +/- 11.02 degrees compared to 63.97 +/- 10.55 degrees in the limited group (n = 20) (P < 0.001, Effect Size = 1.51).

For single-legged squats, ankle dorsiflexion displacement in the weight-bearing lunge assessment was -30.67 +/- 5.67 degrees for the normal group versus -24.23 +/- 4.49 degrees for the limited group (P < 0.001, Effect Size = 1.86).

Knee varus displacement during single-legged squats differed significantly between normal (13.60 +/- 10.28 degrees) and limited (8.10 +/- 6.32 degrees) weight-bearing lunge groups (P < 0.05, Effect Size = 0.66).

core_principles: Restricted ankle dorsiflexion range of motion (DF-ROM) alters lower extremity movement patterns during functional tasks like squatting.
Weight-bearing lunge (WBL) assessments are more effective than nonweight-bearing (NWB) assessments for identifying ankle DF-ROM limitations that impact squatting kinematics.
Ankle DF-ROM restrictions do not appear to alter lower extremity kinematics during jump-landing tasks that involve an immediate maximal vertical jump recoil.
Visual observation of medial knee displacement (knee-valgus collapse) is associated with limited NWB ankle DF-ROM, but limited ankle DF-ROM does not guarantee altered knee movement patterns.
common_mistakes: Medial knee displacement (knee-valgus collapse) during double-legged squats and single-leg squats.
Greater knee-varus displacement during single-leg squats (SLS) associated with restricted ankle mobility.
specific_findings: Group differences in knee and ankle kinematics during squatting were only present when identifying participants as limited based on WBL ankle DF-ROM measurements.
Fong et al reported 14.386 5.58 of DF-ROM assessed with the knee extended in healthy, physically active individuals.
The study's NWB DF-ROM values with the knee extended were 1.63 86 2.588 for the limited group and 16.78 86 2.168 for the normal group.
The jump-landing task utilized a landing from a 30-cm box followed by an immediate countermovement jump for maximal height.
The study compared two groups of participants: Normal (n = 20) and Limited (n = 20).

core_principles: Limited weight-bearing lunge (WBL) ankle dorsiflexion range of motion (DF-ROM) restricts sagittal-plane displacement at both the knee and ankle, leading to smaller peak knee-flexion angles and shallower squat depth.
A heel lift can improve knee mechanics and eliminate medial knee displacement by increasing the tibial angle in the anterior direction.

Limited ankle dorsiflexion can cause compensatory movements in the foot and ankle, such as excessive rearfoot pronation, calcaneal eversion, and talar-head adduction/plantar flexion, forcing the foot to move in the frontal plane to achieve stability.
Greater ankle dorsiflexion during weight-bearing tasks is associated with increased knee-varus displacement during single-legged squats, which helps avoid risky knee-valgus alignment.

Decreased knee flexion during squatting or landing tasks increases ACL loading by creating a larger patellar tendon-tibial shaft angle, which produces greater anterior tibial shear force during quadriceps contraction.
An erect posture (decreased knee flexion) reduces the ability of the hamstrings to offset anterior tibial shear forces and protect the ACL.
common_mistakes: Medial knee displacement (knee valgus) during double-legged squats.
Excessive rearfoot pronation, calcaneal eversion, and talar-head adduction/plantar flexion due to restricted sagittal-plane ankle mobility.
Squatting with restricted knee-flexion displacement (an excessively erect posture) caused by limited ankle dorsiflexion.
specific_findings: A 2-in (5.08-cm) heel lift eliminated medial knee displacement during a double-legged squat.
The heel lift decreased muscle activation during the descent phase of the squat in the gastrocnemius by 32% and the tibialis anterior by 55%.
The effect sizes for differences in knee and ankle displacements between normal and limited weight-bearing lunge (WBL) groups ranged from 1.31 to 1.86.
Placing a 12 8 wedge (12-degree wedge) under the participant's forefoot to restrict dorsiflexion resulted in reduced knee-flexion displacement during a double-legged squat.
Weight-bearing lunge (WBL) ankle DF-ROM predicted anterior-reach distance during the Star Excursion Balance Test with an R^2 value of 0.28 (R 2 ¼ 0.28).
